6.38.m: Mahādeva said: / Once upon a time, my son, I went into the presence of Viṣṇu; / there the glorification arising from dvādaśī was previously asked by me.
Nārada said: / What kind is the supreme Mahādvādaśī, O Mahādeva? / What is the fruit of its vow? Tell me, O Lord of all, O master!
Śiva said: / This ekādaśī, O sage, bestows the fruit of great merit; / conjoined with asterisms, it should be observed by the best of sages.
Jayā, Vijayā, Jayantī, and Pāpanāśinī— / these take away all sins and should be observed by those who desire the fruits.
When the asterism on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight is Punarvasu, / it is called by the name Jayā, the best lunar day among lunar days.
Fasting on it, a man is freed from sin; of this there is no doubt. / And when on the bright twelfth day the asterism is Śravaṇa,
it is celebrated as Vijayā, the best lunar day among lunar days, / on which a gift is multiplied a thousandfold, as is the feeding of brahmins.
Likewise, a fire oblation and fasting grant more than a thousandfold fruit. / And when on the bright twelfth day the asterism is Prājāpatya,
it is called by the name Jayantī, a lunar day that takes away all sins. / Sins committed in seven lifetimes, whether small or great,
Govinda washes away when worshipped on it, surely. / And when on the bright twelfth day the asterism is Puṣya,
then it becomes greatly meritorious, the destroyer of sins. / He who gives a prastha of sesame seeds every single year,
and he who fasts on that [day]—these are remembered as equal. / On that day the Lord of the world, God Hari, the master of all, being pleased,
becomes visibly present indeed; infinite fruit is remembered therein. / It was accomplished by Sagara, Kakutstha, and Nahuṣa;
worshipped on that day, Kṛṣṇa gave them everything on earth. / From vocal, mental, or especially bodily sins,
committed across seven lifetimes, one is freed—of this there is no doubt. / Having fasted on that single [day] conjoined with an auspicious asterism,
a human being obtains the fruit of a thousand ekādaśīs. / Bathing, giving, silent recitation, fire oblation, Vedic study, and worship of the deity—
whatever little is done on it is remembered to have imperishable fruit. / Therefore, this should be performed diligently by those desiring fruits.
When bathed after the fifth horse sacrifice, the righteous Yudhiṣṭhira / inquired of Kṛṣṇa, the crest-jewel of the Yadu lineage.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: / Of the complete fast, of eating only at night, and of eating only once a day, O Lord, / tell me all the merit and the fruit thereof, O Janārdana.

The Blessed Lord said: / When the cold season has arrived in the beautiful month of Mārgaśīrṣa, / on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight, O son of Pṛthā, one should fast on it, / having eaten only once on the tenth day, with a pure mind and firm in vows.
And likewise, understanding the nakta [meal] on the tenth [lunar day], ever self-restrained / in the eighth part of the day, when the sun has grown weak,
one should know that to be the nakta; the nakta is not eating at night. / For a householder, the nakta is prescribed upon seeing the stars;
for an ascetic, it is in the eighth part of the day; at night it is forbidden to him. / Then, having undertaken the observance in the morning, the practitioner of the vow,
and pure, O Pārtha, should perform bathing at midday. / Bathing in a small well is lowest, and bathing in a stepped well is mediocre;
bathing in a pond is best, and bathing in a river is superior to that. / Where living creatures are troubled when one is standing in the water,
upon bathing there, O Pārtha, sin and merit become equal. / Bathing at home is also excellent, and one should purify the water.
Therefore, O best of the Pāṇḍavas, one should perform bathing at home: / 'O earth traversed by horses, traversed by chariots, traversed by Viṣṇu,
O clay, take away my sin that was accumulated by me previously!' / Casting aside anger and greed, single-minded and firm in vows,
one should not speak with an outcaste, nor with heretical men, / nor with those devoted to lying, nor with revilers of Brahmins,
nor with other evildoers, those devoted to incestuous unions, / those who steal the property of others, and those who approach the wives of others.
Having worshipped Keśava, one should present the food-offering there; / with a mind endowed with devotion, one should offer a lamp in the house there.
On that day, O Pārtha, one should avoid sleep and sexual intercourse; / one should spend the entire day in the diversion of the Dharmaśāstras.
Having kept vigil at night, endowed with devotion, O best of kings, / one should give a sacrificial gift to the Brahmins and, bowing down, ask for forgiveness.
Just as the dark [fortnight], so also the bright [fortnight]: a twice-born should observe it in this manner by the rule; / O Pārtha, he should not make any distinction concerning Ekādaśī.
Listen indeed to the fruit of him who performs it thus: / If a man bathes at Śaṅkhoddhāra and sees the club-bearing God,
it does not equal a sixteenth part of the fast of Ekādaśī. / He who gives four hundred thousand [cows] at the solstices and equinoxes, O best of kings,
does not equal a sixteenth part of the fast of Ekādaśī. / The merit that exists at the sacred field of Prabhāsa during an eclipse of the moon or the sun,
that fruit surely accrues to one who fasts on Ekādaśī. / Having drunk water at Kedāra, there is no rebirth;
and likewise, O Pārtha, Ekādaśī brings about the destruction of dwelling in the womb. / The fruit that one may obtain on earth from a horse sacrifice,
the merit of one who fasts on Ekādaśī is a hundred times greater than that. / In whose house ascetics and best of Brahmins eat,
that fruit surely accrues to one who fasts on Ekādaśī. / The merit that is obtained by giving a thousand cows to one who has reached the end of the Vedānta,
the merit of one who fasts on Ekādaśī is a hundred times greater than that. / Those who fast on Ekādaśī are equal to those in whose bodies
the three gods—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—dwell. / Those men are performers of meritorious deeds who are devotees, worshippers of Hari.
There is no reckoning the merit even of the Ekādaśī vow; / to him belongs that merit which is difficult to attain even for the gods.
Half of this merit is obtained from eating the nakta [meal]; / half the merit of the nakta accrues to embodied beings from eating a single meal.
Sacred fords, gifts, and observances roar only as long / as a creature does not fast on the day beloved of Viṣṇu.
Therefore, O best of the Pāṇḍavas, perform this vow! / I do not know the number of the merit concerning which you ask, O Pāṇḍava.
For this has been told, O Pārtha, which is a secret, supreme vow; / there is nothing equal to Ekādaśī, even having performed a thousand sacrifices."
Yudhiṣṭhira said: / "How did that meritorious lunar day of Ekādaśī arise, O God? / How is it sacred in this universe, and how is it dear to the deity?"
The Blessed Lord said: / "Formerly in the Kṛta age, O Pārtha, there was a Dānava named Mura, / very wondrous, exceedingly terrible, terrifying to all the gods.
Even Indra was vanquished by him, as were all the gods, O king, / by that great Asura, like Death itself, evil-minded.
Expelled from heaven by him, they wandered upon the surface of the earth; / filled with apprehension and terrified with fear, they all went to Maheśvara.
Everything was told by Indra before the Lord: / 'Cast out from the world of heaven, they wander upon the surface of the earth.
Remaining among mortals, the gods do not shine, O Maheśvara; / tell me a means, O God, as to what destination the immortals shall reach.'
Mahādeva said: / 'O king of gods, best of deities, where the Garuḍa-bannered Lord resides, / the refuge, the Lord of the Universe, the protector, the supreme refuge,
go there, O best of deities! He will provide protection for you.' / Having heard the word of the Lord, the wise king of gods,
accompanied by the thirty [gods], went there where [the Lord was], O Yudhiṣṭhira. / Seeing that club-bearing God asleep in the midst of the waters,
having folded his hands in supplication, Indra uttered a hymn of praise.
Indra said: / 'Salutations, O Lord of the gods of gods, praised by gods and Dānavas! / O enemy of the Daityas, lotus-eyed one, save us, O Madhusūdana!
All the gods have come, terrified with fear of the Dānava; / you are our refuge, O Lord of the Universe; protect me, O lover of your devotees!
Save us, O Lord of the gods of gods! Save, save us, Janārdana! / Save us indeed, O lotus-eyed one, destroyer of the Dānavas!
All have come into your presence; you alone are our refuge, O Lord! / Render assistance, O Lord, to the gods who have come for refuge!
You are the master, you are the intellect, O God; you are the agent, and you are the cause; / you are the mother of all worlds, you alone are the father of the universe.
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, affectionate to those who come for refuge, / terrified with fear, the deities have come to your refuge.
All the deities have been conquered and cast out of heaven, O Lord, / by the exceedingly fierce Daitya named Mura, of great splendor.' / Hearing Indra's speech, Viṣṇu spoke these words:

The Blessed Lord said: / 'What kind of Dānava is he, O Śakra? What is his form, what kind of strength does he have? / Where is the abode of that wicked one? What is his prowess, what is his valor? / What is the boon of that wicked one? Tell me, O wise one.'
Indra said: / 'Formerly, O Lord of gods, there was born in the lineage of Brahmā / an exceedingly fierce, great Asura named Tālajaṅgha.
His son indeed, renowned as the Dānava named Mura, / is exceedingly violent, of great valor, terrifying to the deities.
There is a city named Candrāvatī; he dwells in that place. / All the deities were conquered and expelled from heaven by him.
Another Indra was installed by him, and another Wind and Fire; / and two others were made the Sun and the Moon, and another Vāyu and Varuṇa.
Everything has been appropriated to himself by him; truly, truly, O Janārdana! / The realm of the gods was made by him completely devoid of its places.'
Hearing that speech of his, Janārdana became enraged: / 'I shall slay the wicked Dānava, who causes terror to the deities.'
Together with the thirty [gods], the God went to the city of Candrāvatī. / The lord of Daityas was seen by the gods roaring again and again.
All the gods were conquered by him and fled in the ten directions. / Seeing Hari, the Dānava spoke: 'Stand, stand!'"

And the Lord, his eyes blood-red with wrath, spoke to him.
The Blessed Lord said:
“O evil-doing Dānava, behold my arm!”

Then all those wicked Dānavas faced Viṣṇu;
struck by his divine arrows, they were overcome with terror.

And the discus was released by Kṛṣṇa into the Daitya armies, O Pāṇḍava;
severed by it by the hundreds, many went to their doom.

Yet one Dānava there fought again and again;
by him all the gods were routed, and Madhusūdana was subdued.

Subdued by that Daitya, a hand-to-hand combat ensued;
he waged hand-to-hand combat for a thousand divine years.

Viṣṇu fell into anxiety, and all the gods fled;
and Viṣṇu, overpowered by him, went to Badarikāśrama.

There was a cave named Siṃhāvatī, and there Janārdana slept;
it was twelve leagues in extent, O Pāṇḍava, and had a single entrance.

Having entered it, he fell fast asleep, and the Dānava was intent on killing [him];
from that very great battle he was weary through Yogamāyā.

Following closely behind, the Dānava then entered the cave;
seeing me asleep there, the Dānava was filled with joy:

“Thinking that Hari has entered here in fear, vanquished by me in this manner,
I will surely slay him who brings fear to the Dānavas.”

A maiden came forth there from Viṣṇu’s body, O Yudhiṣṭhira,
beautiful, exceedingly fortunate, equipped with divine weapons and arms.

Born from a portion of his splendor, possessing great strength and valor,
she was seen by the lord of Dānavas, Mura by name, O Dhanaṃjaya.

A battle was joined by him, challenged by that woman;
the maiden fought there, skilled in all forms of combat.

With roaring shouts, the great Asura named Mura was reduced to ashes;
when that Dānava was slain, the God awakened there.

Seeing the Dānava fallen, he was then filled with wonder:
“By whom has this fierce, terribly formidable enemy of mine been slain?”

“And an exceedingly fierce deed has been done out of compassion for me.”
The maiden said:
“By him the gods, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, serpents, and Rākṣasas,

all headed by Indra, were conquered and expelled from heaven;
I saw Hari asleep, and Mura arrived at his back.

He was about to destroy the three worlds while Janārdana slept.”
Hearing her word, Viṣṇu spoke these words:

“When even I was subdued by him, how was he conquered by you?”
Ekādaśī said:
“O Lord, it is by your favor that the great Daitya was slain by me.”

The Blessed Lord said:
“Joy has come to the sages and the gods in the three worlds.
Tell me, auspicious one, what pleases your heart;
I shall grant it without a doubt, even that which is difficult for the gods to attain.”

Ekādaśī said:
“If you are pleased with me, O God, as truly spoken, O Janārdana,
I desire one boon in my heart, O Lord of the world.

I pray, O Lord of gods, for what is wished by me, O Lord;
if truly, O Lord of the universe, you grant me three promises.”

The Blessed Lord said:
“Truly, truly it has been spoken by me; it shall certainly be yours, O woman of good vows.
Three promises have been given by me, and my word shall not fail here.”

Ekādaśī said:
“In the three worlds, O Lord of gods, and in the four cosmic ages now,
make me like that everywhere in the three worlds, O Lord:

foremost among all sacred places, destroying all obstacles,
granting all spiritual accomplishments—may I become that goddess by your favor!

Those who fast for me with devotion, with devotion to you, O Janārdana,
may all spiritual accomplishments be theirs, if you are pleased with me, O Lord.

Whosoever observes a complete fast, an evening meal, or a single meal [for me],
grant him wealth, dharma, and liberation, O Mādhava.”

Those who are my devotees in the world, and those who are devotees in Kārttika,
are renowned in the four cosmic ages throughout the three worlds, O Lord.

And I consider you my power; established in the Ekādaśī observance,
they will worship me and attain liberation; of this there is no doubt.

Having granted this boon to her, three promises without a doubt,
Ekādaśī, of great vows, became joyful and thriving.

[Viṣṇu said:] “You slay the enemy, and you grant the supreme state;
you destroy all obstacles, bestowing boons of all spiritual accomplishments.

In both fortnights, O son of Pṛthā, the auspicious Ekādaśī is equal;
one should make no distinction between the bright and dark fortnights.

No distinction should be made by all who perform the observance.
Whether by day or by night, one who is intent on devotion listens [to this],

it becomes a single lunar day in both fortnights.
If both parts of Ekādaśī are small, and Trayodaśī appears at the end,

while in the middle Dvādaśī is complete, touching all three, that [day] is dear to Hari;
one should fast on that single [day], [reaping] the fruit of a thousand Ekādaśīs.

Indeed, it is multiplied a thousandfold when the fast is broken on Dvādaśī.
The eighth, the eleventh, the sixth, the third, and the fourteenth:

one should not observe them overlapping the preceding day; one should fast when they overlap the following.
If Ekādaśī lasts for a day and night, and a fraction of an hour remains at dawn,

that lunar day must be avoided; the fast must be observed combined with Dvādaśī.
Such has been declared by me for both fortnights.

One should certainly observe the fast on Ekādaśī, without a doubt;
they go to the Vaiṣṇava realm where the Garuḍa-bannered Lord resides.

Blessed are those mortals in the world devoted to Viṣṇu's devotion,
and whoever recites the glorification of Ekādaśī at all times,

that mortal obtains the meritorious fruit of a thousand cows.
Those who listen with devotion, whether by day or by night,

6.39.m:
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
“I bow to Viṣṇu, the omnipresent Lord manifest, who brings joy to the three worlds,
the Lord of the universe, the creator of the universe, the ancient Supreme Person.

I ask, O God of gods, for a great doubt has arisen in me,
for the benefit of all people and for the purpose of destroying sins:

The Ekādaśī that occurs in the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa—
what is its name, what is its ritual, and what deity is worshipped there?
Explain this to me in detail and faithfully, O Lord.”

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
“You have asked well, O King; good and spotless is your renown!
I shall describe to you, O king of kings, that supreme day of Hari.

She was born in the dark fortnight, on Dvādaśī, dear to me;
[called] Utpatti in Mārgaśīrṣa, born from my body,

born for the destruction of the enemies of the gods, O bull of the Bharatas.
Indeed, she has already been described by me before you, O best of kings.

She is the first Ekādaśī, O King, in the three worlds of moving and unmoving beings,
in the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, named Utpatti.”
Beyond this, I will speak of the [ekādaśī] that falls in the bright half of Mārgaśīrṣa, / by merely hearing of which one obtains the fruit of a Vājapeya sacrifice.
She is named Mokṣā, the supreme destroyer of all sins. / O king, one should diligently worship the god Dāmodara
with tulasī blossoms, with incense and lamps, with utmost effort, / according to the previously stated rule, on the tenth and eleventh [lunar days] likewise.
The ekādaśī named Mokṣā destroys great sins. / A night vigil should be kept for me with dances, songs, and praises.
Listen, O king! I will narrate a divine legendary tale of the Purāṇa, / merely by hearing which destruction of all sins occurs.
If someone's ancestors have gone to a lower birth because of sin, / by dedicating the merit of this [day] to them, they attain liberation, without a doubt.
In the delightful city of Campaka, adorned with Vaiṣṇavas, / a king named Vaikhānasa protected his subjects like his own children.
Many brāhmaṇas who had mastered the Vedas and Vedāṅgas lived [there]; / indeed, the subjects of that King Vaikhānasa were prosperous.
As he was thus ruling his realm, in the middle of the night in a dream, / he saw his own ancestors fallen into a lower state of existence, O king.
Having thus seen them all, his mind overwhelmed with astonishment, / he related the event born of the dream to the twice-born.
The king said: / “O twice-born ones, in a dream I saw my own ancestors fallen into hell, / [crying:] ‘Deliver us, O son, from this ocean of hell!’
Speaking thus, they were indeed weeping again and again; / they were seen by me, O best of the twice-born, and because of this I have no happiness.
This great kingdom of mine brings me no joy; / neither horses nor elephants please me at all, O twice-born.
Neither wife nor sons please me, O best of the twice-born! / What shall I do? Where shall I go? My heart is choked.
Speak, O best of the twice-born, of that vow, that discipline of austerity, / by which my ancestors may immediately attain liberation.
For while the son is living, powerful, and noble-minded, / if the father remains in terrible hell, what is the fruit of that son?”
The brāhmaṇas said: / “O king, nearby is the great hermitage of the sage Parvata. / Let him be approached, O tiger among kings, since he knows past and future.”
Hearing their words, the great King Vaikhānasa / then went immediately right there to the hermitage of Parvata.
Surrounded by brāhmaṇas and accompanied by tributary kings, / the best of kings reached the sage's vast hermitage.
There [he saw the sage] surrounded by ascetics skilled in the study of the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, and Sāmaveda, / looking like a second Brahmā.
Beholding that tiger among sages, King Vaikhānasa / bowed down prostrate like a staff and touched the sage's feet.
That sage inquired after his welfare regarding the seven constituents [of the state], / the absence of obstacles in the kingdom, and the king's happiness.
The king said: / “By your favor, O master, there is welfare in my seven constituents. / For those who are devoted to Viṣṇu and the brāhmaṇas, how could there be obstacles?
In a dream, my own ancestors were seen by me residing in hell. / By the power of what merit do they attain liberation, O best of the twice-born?
This is my doubt, O master; I have approached you to ask about it. / Some remedy must surely be performed here, O best of sages.”
Hearing these words, Parvata, the best of sages, / an ascetic equal to Brahmā, became motionless of eye in meditation.
Remaining in meditation for a single muhūrta, he spoke to the king: / “The past deeds of your ancestors have been ascertained, O best of kings.
In a previous life, your father was a kṣatriya proud of his kingdom. / Bound to the duties of kingship, during his wife's fertile period,
having abandoned his own wife, he went to a village on state business. / But your father did not give her the due season.
By the power of that sin, O tiger among kings, your father / has fallen into a dreadful hell along with his ancestors.
Then King Vaikhānasa spoke this again to the sage: / “By the efficacy of what vow, O sage, could liberation be theirs?”
The sage said: / “In the bright half of Mārgaśīrṣa, there is the [ekādaśī] known by the name of Mokṣā. / This vow should be performed by all, and let its merit be dedicated to your father.
By the power of that merit, liberation will be theirs. / This is true, O fortunate one, just like the word of Brahmā.”
Having heard the word of the sage, he returned to his own home; / and indeed, with difficulty the month of Mārgaśīrṣa was reached by him.
King Vaikhānasa, performing that vow according to the word of the sage, / dedicated the merit, along with all [his household], to his father, that protector of the earth.
The moment the merit was given, a rain of flowers fell in heaven; / indeed, the father of Vaikhānasa entered liberation together with his ancestors.
And from the sky he spoke a sacred word to the king: / ‘May it be well, may it be well with you, O son!’ and having spoken thus, he went to heaven.
Whoever thus observes the auspicious Mokṣā ekādaśī, O king, / their sins are destroyed, and upon death they attain liberation.
There is no ekādaśī higher than this one that grants liberation. / I do not know the count of its merit, O king; this vow is pleasing to me.
Equal to a wish-fulfilling jewel, this indeed bestows liberation upon men. / From reciting it or hearing it, one obtains the fruit of a Vājapeya sacrifice.”

6.40.m: Yudhiṣṭhira said: / “In the dark half of Pauṣa, what is the name of the ekādaśī? / What is its procedure? Tell this in detail! / Declare this, O master: which deity is worshipped there?”
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: / “I will tell you, O king of kings, out of the bond of affection for you. / My satisfaction, O king, is not obtained through sacrifices accompanied by abundant gifts
in such a way as my satisfaction comes indeed through the ekādaśī vow. / Therefore, Hari's day should be observed with every effort.
This is true, not false, O expert among the most righteous! / The one in the dark half of Pauṣa is known by name as Saphalā.
On it, one should worship Lord Nārāyaṇa according to rule. / The auspicious ekādaśī should be observed according to the previously stated method.
Just as Śeṣa is among serpents, the eater of serpents among birds, / Viṣṇu among the gods, and the twice-born among two-footed beings,
and just as the lunar day of Ekādaśī is best among vows, O king, / so those people, O king, are ever worshipful to me
who, absorbed in Hari's day, observe the ekādaśī vow. / Endowed with wealth right in this world, at death they attain liberation.
On the Saphalā, O king, one should worship Hari with fruits according to their names: / with coconuts, betel nuts, and citrons,
with limes and pomegranates, and with auspicious myrobalan fruits, / with cloves, jujubes, and especially with mangoes.
One should worship the lord of the gods of gods with incense and lamps as well; / on the Saphalā, one should specifically make a donation of lamps.
And a night vigil should be performed together with Vaiṣṇavas: / as long as an eye winks, so long one should keep vigil in the night.
Hear, O king, the merit of one whose mind is one-pointed: / there is no sacrifice equal to it, nor indeed is there any pilgrimage place equal to it.
All vows, O lord of kings, are not worth a sixteenth part [of it]. / The fruit that is not obtained even by thousands of years of austerities—
that fruit he surely obtains who keeps the vigil. / Listen, O tiger among kings, to the auspicious story of Saphalā.
There was a city named Campāvatī belonging to Māhiṣmata; / and five young sons were born to that royal sage.
Among them, the eldest was ever devoted to great sin: / an adulterer, attached to harlots, and a drinker of liquor.
The wealth of his father was squandered by that evil-doer. / Ever devoted to wicked conduct, he was a slanderer of brahmins;
he constantly reviled Vaiṣṇavas and the gods. / Seeing his son to be such, King Māhiṣmata,
naming him Luṃpaka, excluded him from the royal sons. / He was banished from the kingdom by his father and relatives.
Cast out by his retinue like an enemy, / Luṃpaka, thus abandoned, then thought:
"I have been cast out by my kinsmen, expelled from the kingdom by my father!" / Thinking thus, he then turned his mind to evil:
"I must go into the terrible, dense forest; / and from there I will plunder my father's entire city!"

Having thus made up his mind, Lumpaka, through the working of fate,
departed from that city and went into a dense forest.
Constantly devoted to killing living beings, a treasury of the arts of theft and gambling, / the whole town was robbed by that evil-doer.
Committing theft in the city, he was caught by the night-watchmen; / he said to them: "I am the son of King Māhiṣmata!"
Released by them, that evil-doer went back to the forest, / always delighting in meat and eating the fruit of trees.
The dwelling of that wicked man was near [an image of] Vāsudeva; / an ancient peepal tree, many years old, stood there.
Great divinity resided in that tree in the forest. / Dwelling right there, Luṃpaka remained evil-minded.
After much time had passed, through some accumulation of merit, / on the tenth day of the dark fortnight of Pauṣa,
having eaten the fruits of the trees, afflicted by the cold at night, / the wretched man named Luṃpaka, devoid of clothing, his sight failing,
tormented by excessive cold near Hari's tree, / had neither sleep nor comfort; he became as if his life-breath were gone.
Covering his mouth with his teeth [chattering], he spent the whole night thus; / even at sunrise that wicked man did not regain consciousness.
Luṃpaka remained unconscious on the day of Saphalā; / only when the sun reached the zenith did Luṃpaka regain his senses.

Looking here and there, and afflicted by the cold at that time,
he walked with stumbling feet, limping again and again.
Having gone into the middle of the forest, he was emaciated with hunger and afflicted; / that wicked Luṃpaka had no strength to kill living beings.
Then, O king, Luṃpaka gathered fruits; / by the time he returned there, the sun had set.
Lamenting, "What will become [of me], O father?" / he placed the abundant fruits at the foot of the tree,

He said: "May Lord Hari, the husband of Śrī, be pleased with these fruits!"
Having spoken thus, Lumpaka did not get any sleep at night.
Viṣṇu considered that night of the wicked man as a vigil; / and he considered [the fruits] as worship for Saphalā, O sinless one.
Luṃpaka had accidentally performed this vow; / by the power of that merit, he obtained a kingdom free of thorns.
By the time the sun rose, Viṣṇu departed. / At that moment a bodiless voice arose in the sky and said:
"O son, you will obtain the kingdom through the grace of Saphalā!" / When this word was spoken, he assumed a divine form.
Then his mind became supremely devoted to Viṣṇu, O king; / adorned with the splendor of divine ornaments, he obtained an unmolested kingdom.
He ruled the kingdom in this manner for fifteen years; / he had sons who satisfied his heart and a wife, by the grace of Kṛṣṇa.
Quickly renouncing the kingdom and entrusting it to his son, / he went to the presence of Kṛṣṇa, having gone to which one does not grieve.
A person who thus performs the supreme vow of Saphalā, O king, / attains happiness in this world and, when dead, attains liberation.
Blessed are those mortals in the world who are devoted to Saphalā; / their birth is fruitful, there is no doubt about this.

By reciting, hearing, and observing [it], O ruler of the people, / a mortal obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.

Thus [ends] in the venerable Padma Purāṇa, in the collection of fifty-five thousand verses, in the Uttarakhaṇḍa, in the dialogue between the husband of Umā and Nārada, [the chapter] named The Saphalā Ekādaśī of the Dark Fortnight of Pauṣa,

6.41.m: Yudhiṣṭhira said: / The auspicious Saphalā Ekādaśī has indeed been related by you, O Kṛṣṇa; / speak out of your grace about that which falls in the bright fortnight:
What is its name? What is its ritual? Which deity is worshipped there? / With whom was Hṛṣīkeśa pleased—you yourself, O Puruṣottama?
The blessed Kṛṣṇa said: / Listen, O king, I will explain the bright [Ekādaśī] of Pauṣa; / I speak, O great king, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
It should be observed with effort, O king, according to the previous ritual; / it is named Putradā, supreme, removing all sins.
Nārāyaṇa is its presiding deity, the granter of desires, the giver of perfection; / there is none superior to this in the three worlds, with their moving and unmoving beings.
Hari makes a person learned and renowned. / Listen, O king, I shall relate the supreme story that removes sins.
Formerly in the city of Bhadrāvatī there was a king named Suketumān; / the queen of that king was named Campakā.
By that childless king time was spent in [unfulfilled] hopes; / the king did not obtain a son who would perpetuate his lineage.
For a long time that righteous king pondered: / "What shall I do? Where shall I go? How can I obtain a son?"
King Suketumān found no pleasure in his realm or in his city; / together with his virtuous wife, he was sorrowful every day.
Both of them, husband and wife, were constantly devoted to anxiety and grief. / His ancestors consume the water offered [by him] as lukewarm:
"After the king, we see no one who will gratify us!" / Remembering thus, his ancestors became sorrowful.
Neither kinsmen nor friends, neither ministers nor well-wishers, / nor elephants, horses, and foot-soldiers pleased this king.
Despair was ever present in the mind of that king: / "There is no fruit to the birth of a man who is sonless!
The house of a childless man is empty, his heart is ever grieving; / without a son there is no freedom from debt to the ancestors, gods, and men.
Therefore, with every effort, a man should beget a son; / theirs is fame in this world, and an auspicious state in the other world.
For those performers of meritorious deeds in whose house the birth of a son occurs, / life, health, and prosperity abide in their home."

"The birth of a son takes place in the house of people who perform meritorious deeds.
Without merit, and without devotion to Viṣṇu, O king,

there are no sons or prosperity; such is my firm conviction."
Thinking thus, that king found no peace.

At dawn the king pondered, and then at midnight he pondered.
Ketumān even considered destroying himself.

Then, reflecting on the wretched fate that follows suicide,
and seeing his own body fallen and likewise his sonlessness,

deliberating again with his intellect upon what would be beneficial for himself,
the king mounted a horse and went to a dense forest.

The royal chaplain and all others did not know that the king had departed.
In the deep forest frequented by beasts and birds,

the king then wandered, looking at the forest trees:
banyans, sacred figs, bilva trees, date palms, jackfruit trees,

bakulas, saptaparṇas, tiṃdukas, and tilakas;
the king saw śāla, tāla, tamāla, and pine trees,

iṅgudī and kakubha trees, and likewise śleṣmātaka trees,
śallakīs, karamardas, pāṭalas, and jujube trees,

aśokas, and palāśas; and also jackals, rabbits,
wild cats, buffaloes, porcupines, and yaks.

The king saw serpents half-emerged from ant-hills,
as well as rutting wild elephants accompanied by their calves,

and herd-leaders with four tusks amidst herds of female elephants.
Seeing those elephants, the king thought of his own [elephants].

Moving among them, the king attained beauty;
the king beheld a forest filled with great wonder.

Hearing the cries of jackals along the path, and likewise the hooting of owls,
watching various bears and deer, he wandered in the middle of the forest.

Thus the king surveyed the dense forest as the sun reached mid-sky.
Afflicted with hunger and thirst, the king ran here and there.

His throat parched, the king reflected:
"What action did I commit, that such suffering has befallen me?

Indeed, I gratified the gods with sacrifices and worship,
and likewise pleased the brāhmaṇas with gifts and delicious feasts,

and ever protected the subjects greatly like my own children.
Why has such terrible and severe sorrow befallen me?"

Thus absorbed in thought, the king went forward into the forest;
by the power of his good deeds, he saw an unsurpassed lake.

touched by fish, further adorned with lotuses,
and graced by kāraṇḍava ducks, cakravāka birds, and royal swans,

filled with many crocodiles, fish, and other aquatic creatures.
Near that lake, he saw many hermitages of sages;

the illustrious king saw them, with omens predicting auspiciousness.
Then his right eye twitched, and his right hand

twitched, foretelling an auspicious outcome for the king.
Seeing the sages on its bank chanting Vedic recitations,

the king's son was overcome with great joy.
Descending from that horse, he stood before the sages.

He bowed individually to those sages of celebrated vows,
folding his hands reverently and bowing like a fallen rod again and again.

Those sages also replied: "We are pleased, O king."
The king said: "Who are you here? Please tell me your names.
For what purpose have you gathered? Tell me the truth."

The sages said: "We are the Viśvedevas, O king, and we have come here to bathe.
Māgha has drawn near, on the fifth day from this.

And today, O king, is the eleventh lunar day known as Putradā.
Viṣṇu gives a son to people who observe Putradā."

The king said: "This is indeed my great distress regarding the begetting of a son.
If you are pleased, then please grant me a son."

A sage said: "Today itself is the day called Putradā, O king;
it is renowned as an ekādaśī. Perform this excellent observance.

Then, through our consecration and by the grace of Keśava,
you will certainly obtain a son, O best of kings."

Following this advice of theirs, the king observed the excellent vow
according to the rite of Putradā, by the instruction of the sages.

Having broken his fast on the twelfth lunar day and bowed repeatedly to the sages,
the king returned home, and then the queen conceived a child.

At the time of delivery, an illustrious son was born through his meritorious deed;
he brought joy to his father and became a protector of the people.

Therefore, O king, the excellent vow of Putradā should be observed.
For the welfare of mankind, this has been related by me to you.

Those mortals who single-mindedly observe the Putradā vow
obtain sons in this world and, upon death, go to heaven.
From reading or hearing this, O king, one attains the fruit of an Agniṣṭoma sacrifice."

6.42.m:
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "Well said, O Kṛṣṇa, Lord of the Universe, primordial deity, Lord of the World!
Speak out of your grace; show mercy upon me.

Which ekādaśī occurs in the dark fortnight of Māgha?
What is its name and what is its rule? Tell this in detail."

The Blessed Lord said: "Listen, O tiger among kings, to the one that occurs in the dark fortnight of Māgha;
it is renowned as Ṣaṭtilā, destroying all sins.

Listen to the auspicious story of Ṣaṭtilā that removes sin,
which Pulastya, the best of sages, recounted to Dālabhya."

Dālabhya said: "Creatures who have arrived in the mortal world commit sin,
and are burdened with sins such as the killing of a brāhmaṇa and diverse others.

They steal others' wealth and are infatuated by other vices.
How do they not go to hell, O holy one? Tell me that in truth.

O lord, you should tell me this:
how can sin reach pacification easily, through some small gift?"

Pulastya said: "Well said, well said, O highly fortunate one! This is a profound secret, very difficult to obtain,
which has not been revealed to anyone by the deities Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Indra.

That I shall declare, questioned as I am by you, O best of the twice-born.
When the month of Māgha has arrived, pure, bathed, and with senses restrained,

free from desire, anger, arrogance, envy, greed, and slander,
remembering the God of gods, and having washed his feet with water,

a man should take cow-dung that has not fallen on the ground,
and, casting sesame seeds and cotton into it, he should make balls.

One hundred and eight of them indeed—no doubt should be entertained here.
Then, when Māgha has arrived, if there should be the constellation Āṣāḍhā,

or Mūla, of the dark fortnight, he should then undertake
the rules of the ekādaśī at an auspicious time. Hear its procedure from me.

Having thoroughly worshipped the God of gods, well bathed, disciplined, and pure,
and having praised the names of Kṛṣṇa whenever he stumbles or the like,

he should keep a vigil at night and first cause a fire oblation to be performed.
On the second day, he should worship Hari again, the Lord of the God of gods,

with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and an offering of kṛsara;
and then, remembering him again and again by the name of Kṛṣṇa,"

With ash gourds, coconuts, or indeed with citrons,
or, if all these are lacking, O lord of Brahmins, surrounded by auspicious betel nuts,
one should offer arghya according to rule after worshipping Janārdana:

“O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa! You are compassionate; be the refuge of those without refuge!
Have mercy, O Puruṣottama, on those sunk in the ocean of worldly existence!

Homage to you, O lotus-eyed one! Homage to you, source of the universe!
O friend of Brahmins, homage be to you, O Supreme Person, firstborn!
Accept the arghya offered by me, together with Lakṣmī, O Lord of the universe!”

Thus ends the argha mantra.
Then one should worship a brahmin and present a water-pot,
parasol, sandals, and clothes, saying: "May Kṛṣṇa be pleased with me!"

A black cow should be given to an excellent Brahmin according to one’s ability;
a vessel of sesame seeds should be given, O best of Brahmins, by one discerning of recipients.

for so many thousands of years he is glorified in the heavenly world.
Bathing with sesame, anointing with sesame, offering sesame into fire, giving water with sesame,

giving sesame, and eating [sesame]—these six sesames destroy sin.
Nārada said:
O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, mighty-armed one! Homage to you, source of the universe!

Formerly, in the mortal world, there was a certain Brahmin woman, O Nārada,
constantly devoted to the practice of vows, always devoted to the worship of the gods.

Devoted to month-long fasts, and always my devotee,
engaged in fasting for Kṛṣṇa, dedicated to my worship,

her body was indeed emaciated by fasts, O best of Brahmins.
Out of devotion to gods, Brahmins, and unmarried maidens,

that greatly chaste woman continually gave away houses and the like,
yet she was constantly devoted to extreme austerities, O Brahmin.
Alms were not given to mendicants, nor were Brahmins gratified [with food].

Then, after a great deal of time, it was thought by me, O Brahmin:
“Her body is indeed purified by severe vows, without a doubt;

the Vaiṣṇava realm has indeed been honoured by her through physical mortification,
yet the gift of food has not been given, by which supreme satisfaction might arise.”

Knowing this, O Brahmin, I arrived in the mortal world;
assuming the form of an ascetic with a skull-bowl, she was asked for alms:

“From where have you come, O Brahmin? Where are you going? Speak before me!”
Again it was said by me, “Give alms, O beautiful one!”

With great anger, a lump of clay was thrown by her into the copper vessel,
whereupon, O Brahmin, I went back to heaven.

Then, after a great deal of time, that female ascetic of very great vows
came to heaven in her very body by the power of her practice of vows.

By giving the lump of clay, a charming house was obtained,
and yet, O Brahmin-sage, it was completely devoid of heaps of grain.

As she inspected the house, she saw nothing there;
then she went out of the house and came before me, O Brahmin.

Overcome with great anger, she spoke this word:
“By me, through vows, severe penances, and manifold fasts,

the god, the protector of the whole world, was propitiated with worship;
yet nothing is seen there in my house, O Janārdana!”

Then it was said by me to her: “Go home, O woman of great vows!
Filled with curiosity, they will surely come—

the wives of the gods, filled with wonder, indeed to see you.
Do not open the door except in return for their reciting the merits of Ṣaṭtilā.”

Having been spoken to thus by me, that mortal woman went then;
meanwhile, the wives of the gods arrived, O Brahmin.

And it was said by them there: “We have indeed come to see you.
Open the door for yourself today, O fair one, so that we may see you!”

The mortal woman said:
“If I am to be seen, the truth must be spoken in particular:
the sacred vow of Ṣaṭtilā, for the purpose of opening the door.”

Then, opening the door, the mortal woman was seen by them;
she was not a goddess, nor a Gandharva woman, nor an Asura woman, nor a serpent woman.

Never before had such a woman been seen as this one was, O bull among Brahmins.
By the instruction of the goddess, the vow of Ṣaṭtilā was performed

by that mortal woman of true vows, which bestows the fruit of enjoyment and liberation.
Endowed with beauty and radiance, in an instant she attained [abundance]:

wealth, grain, garments and the like, gold and silver as well,
a mansion supplied with everything, by the power of Ṣaṭtilā.
Endowed with beauty and radiance, she was transformed in an instant.

Excessive greed should not be harboured; one should abandon miserliness with wealth.
According to one's own wealth, one should cause sesame seeds and garments to be given.

And thus a man obtains freedom from disease in birth after birth;
neither poverty, nor hardship, nor misfortune

shall occur, O best of Brahmins, by fasting on Ṣaṭtilā.
By this rite, O king, a giver of sesame, without a doubt,

6.43.m:
Yudhiṣṭhirā said:
Well spoken by you, O Kṛṣṇa! You are the primal god, O Lord!
Beings born of sweat, born of eggs, born of sprouts, and born of wombs—

you are their creator, transformer, protector, and destroyer.
In the dark fortnight of Māgha, Ṣaṭtilā was told by you;

and which one occurs in the bright fortnight, O God? Tell by your grace!
What is its name, what is its procedure, and which deity is worshipped there?

purifying and sin-destroying, granting desires and granting liberation to mortals,
destroying [the sin of] killing a Brahmin, and destroying the state of being a piśāca.

When its vow is observed, the state of a ghost does not occur to mortals at all;
there is none higher than this, sin-destroying and conferring liberation.

For this reason, O king, it should be observed with diligence.
Let the auspicious Purāṇic story be heard, O tiger among kings!

In the Lotus Purāṇa, its greatness has been related by me.
Once in the heavenly world, Indra indeed exercised his rule.

There the gods were living in comfort in a delightful [place],
devoted to drinking nectar, attended by hosts of apsarases.

There was the Nandana grove, attended by Pārijāta trees;
there the gods delight and sport with apsarases.

Once, sporting at his will, O king, that lord of the gods,
the ruler of fifty crores, caused dancing out of joy.

There the Gandharvas sing: the Gandharva Puṣpadanta,
and Citrasena was right there, and likewise the daughter of Citrasena;

and there was the woman named Mālinī, the wife of Citrasena,
and born of Mālinī was [a daughter] named Puṣpadantī.
Puṣpadanta had a son named Mālyavān. / Mālyavān was utterly infatuated with the beauty of Puṣpadantī.
Indeed, Mālyavān was captivated by her side-glances. / Behold her beauty, endowed with grace and loveliness!
Her arms seemed made by the god of love as nooses for the neck; / her eyes stretched to her ears, revolving with red corners.
Her ears were radiant with earrings, O best of kings; / she had a conch-like neck and was adorned with divine ornaments.
Her breasts were full and raised, like two golden pitchers; / the waist of that slender-limbed girl was thin, graspable with a fist, unsurpassable.
Her buttocks were broad, and the region of her hips expansive; / her feet were splendid, shining like red water-lilies.
Mālyavān was deeply infatuated with Puṣpavatī, who was of such [beauty]. / The two came together to dance for the pleasure of Śakra.
While the two were singing there, attended by the host of Apsarases, / the limbs of Puṣpadantī and Mālyavān were overcome by passion.
Through mutual passion they fell under the sway of bewilderment. / With their minds confused, they could not sing the song accurately.
With their gazes thus fixed on each other, fallen under the power of the arrows of love, / the chief of gods realized that their minds were united there.
Considering his own disrespect / due to the lapse in rhythm and musical tempo, and the abandoning of the song,
Maghavan, enraged on their account, pronounced this curse: / 'Fie, fie on you two, fallen fools, transgressors of my command!
May you two become piśācas, maintaining the status of husband and wife, / and reach the mortal world, experiencing the fruit of your action!'
Thus cursed by Maghavan, both sorrowful in mind, / bewildered by Indra's curse, they reached Mount Himavat.
Both fell into the state of piśācas, suffering terrible misery. / Agonized in mind there, both entered extreme hardship in the snow.
Bewildered, they did not remember their status as Gandharva and Apsaras; / they were tormented by heat arising from their physical lapse.
Afflicted by their deeds, they found no comfort or peace at night; / disputing with one another, they roamed in the mountain cave.
Tormented by the cold produced by the snow, / their bodies had hair standing on end, and their teeth chattered.
Then that male piśāca spoke to his wife, the female piśāca: / 'What great, terrible, hair-raising sin was committed [by us],
by which this state of piśāca was obtained through our own wicked deed? / Considering this piśāca state to be a terrible hell, causing misery,
one should therefore by every effort avoid committing sin.' / Absorbed in such reflections, the two remained there, emaciated with grief.
By the power of fate, there arrived for them the eleventh lunar day of Māgha, / renowned as Jayā, the best among lunar days.
When that day arrived, O king, / the two remained there destitute of food and without drinking water.
No killing of living beings was done, nor was there eating of leaves and fruits. / They were near a sacred fig tree, continually filled with sorrow.
As they remained in that very manner, O king, the sun set, / and the dreadful, terrible, life-stealing night arrived.
Trembling, the two then slept on the ground, / clinging to each other with their limbs and arms.
They found neither sleep nor pleasure there, nor any happiness. / Thus, O tiger among kings, were they tormented by Indra's curse.
As they were thus miserable, the night passed away. / The sun rose at the arrival of the twelfth day.
O tiger among kings, their liberation was conceived in my heart: / the excellent observance of Jayā had been performed, and an all-night vigil was kept.
Therefore, hear how it happened through the power of the observance: / when the twelfth day arrived and the observance of Jayā had thus been performed,
by Viṣṇu's power, O king, their state of piśāca departed. / Puṣpadantī and Mālyavān regained their former forms.
Endowed with their former love and wearing their former ornaments, / they mounted a celestial vehicle and went to charming heaven.
Approaching the lord of gods, they joyfully bowed before him. / Seeing them in such a state, Maghavan spoke in astonishment:
Indra said: / 'Tell me, by what merit has your piśāca state disappeared? / Having received my curse, by which god were you released?'
Mālyavān said: / 'By the grace of Vāsudeva and by the observance of Jayā, / our piśāca state has gone, O lord, through the power of devotion to Him.'

Hearing this, Maghavan then replied in turn:
"You two have become pure and purifying, worthy of homage even by me."
since you have observed the day of Hari and are devoted to Viṣṇu. / Those mortals who are absorbed in the day of Hari and devoted to Kṛṣṇa
are certainly worshipful even to us; there is no doubt. / Sport happily as you please with Puṣpadantī in the abode of the gods.'
Kṛṣṇa said: / 'For this reason, O king, the day of Hari should be observed. / Jayā, O tiger among kings, removes the sin of killing a brahmin.
By him all gifts are given, and all sacrifices are completely / performed, who has observed the vow of Jayā.
He surely rejoices in Vaikuṇṭha for ten million kalpas. / From reciting or hearing it, O king, one attains the fruit of an Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.'

6.44.m: Yudhiṣṭhira said: / 'In the dark fortnight of Phālguna, what is the name of the Ekādaśī? / Please tell me, O Vāsudeva, out of your grace.'

The venerable Kṛṣṇa said: / 'Nārada questioned Brahmā, who is seated on the lotus: / "In the dark fortnight of Phālguna, [the Ekādaśī] named Vijayā occurs; / O best of the twice-born, graciously relate its merit."'
Brahmā said: / 'Listen, Nārada, I will narrate the supreme tale that removes sins, / this observance of Vijayā, which I have not revealed to anyone.
For this ancient observance is pure and destroys sins; / it bestows victory upon kings, without a doubt.
Formerly, Rāma went to the forest for fourteen years. / Accompanied by Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, he dwelt in Pañcavaṭī.
While Rāma of victorious nature was living right there, / his illustrious wife Sītā was abducted by Rāvaṇa out of lust.
Through that grief, Rāma too fell into despair at that time. / Wandering about, he then saw Jaṭāyus, whose life had ended.
Then Kabandha was slain by him as he wandered in the midst of the forest. / His friendship was established together with Sugrīva.
Armies of monkeys assembled for Rāma's sake, / and then Jānakī was seen in the garden of Laṅkā by Hanumat.
Rāma's token of recognition was given to her, and a great feat was performed. / Returning, he reported everything there to Rāma.
Then, hearing the words of Hanumat, / Rāmacandra resolved upon departure with the approval of Sugrīva.'

“O Saumitri, by what religious merit can the ocean, the abode of Varuṇa, be crossed? / It is fathomless, thoroughly agitated, and teeming with aquatic monsters. / I see no means at all by which it can be easily crossed.”
Lakṣmaṇa said: / “You alone are the primeval God, the ancient Puruṣottama. / Yet the sage Baka Dālbhya resides here in the midst of an island.
His hermitage is half a yojana from this place, O Rāghava; / and there are many other brāhmaṇas there, O delight of the Raghu lineage.
Go and ask that ancient, eminent sage, O king of kings.” / Having heard these most excellent words of Lakṣmaṇa,
Rāghava went to see the great sage Baka Dālbhya. / Rāma bowed his head to the sage, like an immortal to Viṣṇu.
The sage, knowing Rāma to be the ancient Puruṣottama / who had entered a human body for a particular purpose,
the pleased sage said, “From where have you come, Rāma?”
Rāma said: / “By your favor, O brāhmaṇa, I have come with my army / to the shore of the lord of rivers to conquer Laṅkā with its rākṣasas.
Through your benevolence, by what means can the ocean be crossed by me? / Tell me that means, O sage; grant your grace right now.
For this very reason have I come here to see you.” / Hearing the words of Rāma, the great sage Baka Dālbhya,
with a delighted mind, said to lotus-eyed Rāma: / “You must perform today, O Rāma, the most excellent of all vows,
by the performance of which victory will swiftly be yours. / Having conquered Laṅkā and the rākṣasas, you will attain pure renown.
With an attentive mind, undertake this vow. / In the dark fortnight of the month of Phālguna occurs the Vijayā Ekādaśī.
By the vow of that [day], O Rāma, your victory will be assured; / without doubt you will cross the sea together with the monkeys.
Hear the rule, O king, that yields the fruit of this vow: / When the tenth day has arrived, one should have a water jar prepared,
made of gold, silver, copper, or clay; / adorned, filled with water, and adorned with sprouts, one should install it.
One should place the seven grains beneath it, and barley on top of it. / Upon that, one should install the divine Lord, the golden Nārāyaṇa.
When the eleventh day arrives, one should take a morning bath; / one should place the jar steadily, with garlands on its neck and with unguents.
One should especially worship it with betel nuts and coconuts, / with perfumes, incenses, lamps, and various food-offerings.
In front of the jar, O Rāma, that day is spent with virtuous discourses and the like; / and at night, a wise person should keep vigil before it.
One should light a lamp of clarified butter for the sake of the unbroken vow. / When the twelfth day arrives and the sun has risen,
having taken the jar to a watery place—a river, a mountain stream, / or a pond—and having set it down and worshipped it according to rule,
one should give that jar along with the deity to a brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas; / along with the jar, O king of kings, one should bestow great gifts.
According to this rite, O Rāma, joined together with your troop commanders, / perform the vow diligently, and victory will be yours.”

Hearing this, Rāma then did as had been told;
when the vow was performed, that joy of the Raghus became victorious.
Sītā was regained, Laṅkā conquered, and Rāvaṇa slain in battle. / Those men who perform this vow according to this rite, O son,
attain victory in this world and imperishable status in the next world. / For this reason, O son, the Vijayā vow should be performed.
The glorification of the Vijayā destroys all sins; / by reciting it and hearing it, one obtains the fruit of a Vājapeya sacrifice.

Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, named "The Glorification of Vijayā of the Dark Fortnight of Phālguna," in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the compilation of fifty-five thousand [verses].

6.45.m: [Yudhiṣṭhira] said: / “The great-fruited glorification of the dark fortnight's Vijayā has been heard; / now tell of the one that is called by name in the bright fortnight of Phālguna.”
The holy Kṛṣṇa said: / “O highly fortunate son of Dharma, listen, I shall now tell you / what was spoken by the magnanimous Vasiṣṭha when questioned by Māndhātṛ.
A particular [vow] for Phālguna has been declared with special merit, O king: / the holy Āmalakī vow, which bestows the fruit of the world of Viṣṇu.
Going beneath an āmalakī tree, one should keep vigil there. / Having kept vigil at night, one obtains the fruit of [gifting] a thousand cows.”
Māndhātṛ said: / “When indeed did this āmalakī tree originate, O best of the twice-born? / Explain all this to me; indeed, my curiosity is very great.
Why is it pure, and why does it destroy sin? / Why, having kept vigil, does one obtain the fruit of a thousand cows?”
Vasiṣṭha said: / “I shall tell, O highly fortunate one, how this great āmalakī tree, / the destroyer of all sins, came to be on earth.
Formerly, when the single cosmic ocean had arisen and all moving and unmoving things had perished, / when the hosts of gods and demons had perished, and the serpents and rākṣasas had been destroyed,
the Lord of the foremost gods, the eternal Supreme Self, / entered the supreme Brahman, His own imperishable state.
Then, as He was awake, from His mouth a drop resembling the moon in luster / was produced from a spit, and it fell to the earth.
From that drop arose of itself the great dhātrī tree, / rich with boughs and branches, bent down by the weight of its fruit.
It is proclaimed as the first-grown of all trees. / Then, after that, these creatures were created by Brahmā.
The divine Lord created gods, dānavas, gandharvas, / yakṣas, rākṣasas, serpents, and spotless great sages.
Those gods came there where the dhātrī tree, dear to Hari, stood; / seeing it, O highly fortunate one, they fell into supreme wonder.
Standing together and pondering, they thought, ‘We do not recognize this tree.’ / As they were pondering thus, a bodiless voice spoke:
‘This āmalakī tree is the foremost, considered sacred to Viṣṇu. / By the mere remembrance of it, one obtains the fruit born of gifting cows.
By touching it the merit is doubled, and by wearing it, tripled. / Therefore, with all effort, the āmalakī is always to be resorted to.
It is declared to remove all sins, sacred to Viṣṇu, destroying wickedness. / At its base resides Viṣṇu, and above him the Grandfather [Brahmā].
On the trunk rests the divine Rudra, the Supreme Lord; / on the boughs are all the sages, and on the branches are the deities.
The gods sit on the leaves, and the Maruts on the flowers; / the lords of creatures are situated in the fruits.
Thus the dhātrī is declared by me to consist of all the gods; / therefore it is most worthy of worship by those devoted to Viṣṇu.’
The sages said: / ‘Who are you? We do not know. How have you become the cause? / Whether you are a god or someone else, tell us truthfully.’
The voice said: / ‘He who is the creator of all beings and of all the worlds everywhere, / seeing the wise astonished—I am that eternal Viṣṇu.’
Hearing that speech of the God of gods, the sons of Brahmā / set about praising that beginningless and endless God there:
‘Homage to the Self who is the self of all beings, to the Supreme Self; / homage always to Acyuta, homage, homage to Ananta!’”
"Salutations, salutations to Dāmodara, the wise seer, the lord of sacrifice!" / Thus praised by the sages, the blessed Hari was pleased.
He replied to those great sages: "What desired boon shall I give you?" / The sages said: / "If you are pleased, O Blessed One, out of a wish for our welfare,
explain a vow that yields heaven and liberation as its fruit, / that grants wealth and grain, is meritorious, and brings satisfaction to oneself,
involving little exertion, bearing great fruit, the best among vows, / by the performance of which, O Lord of gods, one is honored in the world of Viṣṇu."
Viṣṇu said: / "If in the bright fortnight of Phālguna the twelfth [lunar day] falls with the Puṣya nakṣatra, / that [day] is exceedingly meritorious, destroying the greatest sins.
Listen, O best among the twice-born, to the special practice to be performed then: / approaching an āmalakī tree, one should observe a vigil there.

Freed from all sins, one obtains the fruit of [gifting] a thousand cows. / This, O brahmins, is described to you as the best among vows: / having worshipped Acyuta on that day, one never falls from the world of Viṣṇu."
The sages said: / "Tell [us] the rule of this vow, how it may be completely fulfilled: / what are the mantras, what are the salutations, and which deity is proclaimed?
How is the gift to be made, how the bath, and what is recorded as the ritual of worship? / Tell [us] truly the mantra for offering the arghya and the worship."
Viṣṇu said: / "Listen, O foremost among the twice-born, to the complete rule of this vow: / having remained without food on the eleventh [day], on the following day,
[saying,] 'I shall eat, O Lotus-eyed One; be my refuge, O Acyuta!' / Having thus undertaken the observance, preceded by cleaning the teeth,
one should not converse with fallen men, thieves, or heretics, / nor with men of wicked conduct, breakers of proper bounds, or violators of the guru's wife.
Then in the afternoon, the wise person, with self-restraint, / should perform the bath according to rule in a river, a pond, a well, or at home.
First applying clay, one should then bathe, [reciting:] / 'O earth, traversed by horses, traversed by chariots, traversed by Viṣṇu,
O clay, take away my sin, whatever misdeed has been done by me!'

Thus ends the clay mantra.
"You, O water, are the life of all creatures, the protector of the body
of those born of sweat and of sprouting seeds; homage to the lord of tastes!"
I am bathed in all sacred waterplaces, in pools and waterfalls, / in rivers and gods' excavated ponds; may this be my bath!'"

Thus ends the bath mantra.
And having an image of the sage, the son of Jamadagni, fashioned of gold,
of a māṣaka of gold, or else of half of that half,
coming home, one should perform the worship and fire oblation of the worship. / Then one should go to the āmalakī tree, equipped with all paraphernalia.
Having gone to the āmalakī tree and cleaned all around it, / one should place an unblemished jar with mantras, standing firm,
supplied with the five gems, perfumed with divine scents, / accompanied by a parasol and a pair of sandals, and anointed with white sandalwood,
its neck draped with garlands of flowers, fumigated with every kind of incense; / one should arrange rows of lamps all around, highly enchanting.
Upon it one should set a vessel completely filled with divine parched grain; / on the vessel one should place the god, the son of Jamadagni, of great splendor:
'Salutations to Viśoka' for the two feet, to the Universal-formed for the two knees, / to Ugra for the two thighs, and to Dāmodara for the waist;
the belly to Padmanābha, the chest to the bearer of the Śrīvatsa; / to the Discus-bearer for the left arm, and salutations to the Mace-bearer for the right;
salutations to Vaikuṇṭha for the neck, and the mouth to Yajñamukha; / the nose to Viśokanidhi, and the two eyes to Vāsudeva;
the forehead with 'to Vāmana', salutations to the two eyebrows with 'to Rāma', / and one should worship that head with 'Salutations to the Universal Soul.'

Thus ends the worship mantra.
Then one should offer an argha to the god of the gods
with an unblemished fruit and with a mind filled with devotion.
Then one should keep a vigil with a devout mind, / with dances, songs, musical instruments, stories of dharma, and hymns,
and with Vaiṣṇava narratives one should spend the whole night. / Then one should circumambulate the myrobalan tree reciting the names of Viṣṇu,
one hundred and eight times, or twenty-eight times. / Then at dawn, having performed the waving of lights for Hari,
and having honored a brahmin, one should offer everything to him: / the jar for the son of Jamadagni, the pair of garments, and the two sandals,
[saying,] 'May Keśava be pleased with me in the form of the son of Jamadagni!' / Then, touching the āmalakī tree and circumambulating it,
and bathing according to rule, one should feed brahmins. / Then one may eat oneself, surrounded by one's family.
Whatever merit arises from this being done, all that I tell you: / whatever merit is in all sacred waterplaces, whatever fruit is in all gifts,
and exceeding all sacrifices, one obtains it—there is no doubt here. / All this has been declared to you, the best among vows."
Having spoken this much, the Lord of gods vanished right there. / And those sages too performed everything without omission.

6.45.m:
Likewise you also, O king of kings, best of men, ought to perform / this irresistible vow that frees from all sins.

Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, named "Āmalakī Ekādaśī of the Bright Fortnight of Phālguna," in the conversation between the husband of Umā and Nārada, in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the compilation of fifty-five thousand [verses].

Chapter Forty-Six. Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Āmalakī has been heard about in the bright fortnight of Phālguna;
what is the name of the Ekādaśī in the dark fortnight of Caitra?"

The blessed Kṛṣṇa said: / "Listen, O king of kings, I shall tell the sin-destroying tale / that Lomaśa spoke when questioned by Māndhātṛ, the universal emperor."

in the first fortnight of Caitra, what is the name of the eleventh [lunar day]? / What is the rule, what is its fruit? Speak out of your grace!"

Lomaśa said: / "In the month of Caitra, in the dark fortnight, the eleventh [lunar day] / is indeed proclaimed by the name Pāpamocanī, destroying condition as a piśāca.

Listen, O king, I shall tell its wondrous, auspicious story / that grants wishes, yields success, destroys sins, and bestows dharma.

Formerly, in the Caitraratha region, frequented by groups of apsarases, / when the springtime arrived, in a forest teeming with six-legged bees,

daughters of Gandharvas sported with kinnaras to musical instruments, / and the dwellers of the third heaven, led by Pākaśāsana, were playing.

There was no other forest bringing pleasure like Caitraratha; / in that forest sages were performing intense austerities.

Toward a sage named Medhāvin, an ascetic residing there, / an apsaras set out to delude that best of sages.

Known as Mañjughoṣā, revealing her affection toward him, / she remained out of fear about a krośa away, near his hermitage,

singing sweetly and melodiously, plucking her lute. / Beholding her singing thus, adorned with flowers and sandalwood,

even Kāma, eager for victory over the lords of sages devoted to Śiva, / that son of the mind took up residence in her body.

Making her two eyebrows the curved ends of his bow, her sidelong glance the bowstring, / and making her two eyes with their eyelashes the arrows in due order,

Making her breasts his tent, he set forth for victory; / Mañjughoṣā became the very army of that Kāma.

Seeing the sage Medhāvin, she too was afflicted with desire; / Medhāvin, whose body was bursting with youth, shone brightly.

Endowed with a white sacred thread, he looked like a second god of love. / Medhāvin was living in the auspicious hermitage of Cyavana.

Seeing that best of sages dwelling there, Mañjughoṣā / fell under the sway of love and began to sing very softly.

led forcibly into the power of infatuation by Kāma along with his army, [succumbed]. / Mañjughoṣā approached, and seeing the sage in such a state,

the woman fascinated him with gestures, expressions, and sidelong glances; / setting down her lute, she embraced that lord of sages.

Like a creeper entwining a tree shaken by the force of the wind, / he, Medhāvin, the best of sages, sported with her.

Seeing her excellent body right there, / his knowledge of the truth of Śiva vanished, and he fell under the sway of the principle of desire.

Sporting with her, the lustful sage knew neither night nor day; / much time passed while the sage’s conduct fell into neglect.

Mañjughoṣā prepared to go to the heavenly world. / As she was leaving, she said to the best of sages while he was dallying: / 'Give permission, O brāhmaṇa, for my departure to my own land.'

Medhāvin said: / 'You have arrived only today at twilight, O fair-faced one; / stay near me until the morning twilight.' / Hearing these words of the sage, she became filled with fear.

6.45.m:
Afraid of the sage's curse, O best of kings, / she made love again with that ṛṣi for many years.

For fifty-five years, nine months, and three days / she dallied with the sage, and to him it seemed like only half a night.

When that time had passed, she spoke again to the sage: / 'Give permission, O brāhmaṇa; I must go to my own home.'

Medhāvin said: / 'It is morning now, so listen to my word; / remain steadfast, indeed, as long as I perform the twilight devotion.'

Hearing this statement of the sage, overwhelmed with joy,
smiling slightly, she of pure smiles replied.

The apsaras said: / 'O lord of brāhmaṇas, O sinless one, how long has your twilight devotion lasted? / Show favor to me and consider the time that has passed!'

Hearing her words, his eyes wide with astonishment,
the best of brahmins then took the measure of the time that had passed.

Fifty-seven years had passed with her. / Then he became angry with her, becoming like a wreath of flames.

Emitting sparks from his eyes, exceedingly furious, / seeing her as the embodiment of death who had destroyed his ascetic heat,

6.45.m:
Seeing that the ascetic heat earned with hardship was destroyed with her, / the sage, trembling-lipped and his senses agitated, replied there.

Medhāvin then cursed her: 'Become a female goblin! / Fie on you, wicked, ill-behaved, unchaste woman, fond of sin!'

Burned by his curse, bowed low with humility, / that fair-browed one spoke words to the sage, seeking his grace: / 'Show favor, O lord among brāhmaṇas; grant mitigation of the curse!

Friendship with the virtuous is formed by seven words and steps; / O brāhmaṇa, I have spent many years with you! / For this reason, O master, O observer of good vows, show favor!'

The sage said: / 'Listen to my word, O blessed woman, which grants mitigation of the curse: / What can I do, O sinful one, since my great ascetic heat was brought to ruin by you?

In the dark fortnight of Caitra, there is the auspicious Ekādaśī / named Pāpamocanikā, which destroys all sins.

When its observance is kept, O radiant one, your state as a goblin will depart.' / Having said this, Medhāvin went to his father’s hermitage.

Seeing him arrive, Cyavana said to him: / 'What is this that you have done, son? You have destroyed your merit!'
