6.45.m:
Medhāvin said: / 'Father, a great sin has indeed been committed by me, and an apsaras was enjoyed; / tell me an expiation, father, by which my sin may be destroyed.'

Cyavana said: / 'In the dark fortnight of Caitra, there is indeed the one named Pāpamocanī; / when its observance is performed, O son, the mass of sin will be destroyed.'

Hearing the words of his father, he performed that excellent vow;
his sin went to destruction, and he became endowed with ascetic power.

Mañjughoṣā too, having performed this best of vows, / was completely freed from goblin-hood by the Pāpamocanikā vow; / assuming a divine form, that excellent apsaras went to heaven.

Lomaśa said: / 'O king, the best among men who observe Pāpamocanikā— / whatever sin is theirs, all of that comes to an end.

By reading or hearing [of it], O king, one obtains the fruit of a thousand cows: / the killer of a brāhmaṇa, the stealer of gold, the drinker of liquor, and the violator of the guru's bed—

By performing this vow, they are freed from sin; / for this best of vows yields great merit when performed.'

Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, named "Pāpamocanī Ekādaśī of the Dark Fortnight of Caitra," in the conversation between the husband of Umā and Nārada, in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the compilation of fifty-five thousand [verses].

6.47.m: Yudhiṣṭhira said: / 'O Vāsudeva, obeisance to you! Tell me before me: / In the bright fortnight of Caitra, what is the name of the Ekādaśī?'
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: / 'Listen with one mind, O king, to an ancient, holy story / which Vasiṣṭha formerly told to Dilīpa when he questioned him.'
Dilīpa said: / 'O lord, I wish to hear; please tell me out of favor: / In the month of Caitra, in the bright fortnight, what is the name of the Ekādaśī?'
Vasiṣṭha said: / 'You have asked well, O king! I shall tell it before you: / In the bright fortnight of Caitra, it is known by name as Kāmadā.
It is the most sacred Ekādaśī, a forest fire to the fuel of sins; / hear, O king, this story that destroys sins and bestows merit.
Formerly, in the delightful city of Nāgapura adorned with gold and jewels, / very fierce nāgas, headed by Puṇḍarīka, dwelt.
In that city, Puṇḍarīka ruled as king; / he was served by gandharvas, kinnaras, and apsarases.
The excellent apsaras Lalitā and the gandharva Lalita, / both impassioned with love, were a married couple smitten with desire.
They dallied then in their delightful home filled with wealth and grain; / in Lalitā's heart her husband dwelt at all times,
and in his heart the passionate woman Lalitā dwelt constantly. / Then, once upon a time, Puṇḍarīka was sporting while seated in the assembly;
Lalita was singing songs without his beloved; / his tongue stumbled over the metrical meter as he remembered Lalitā.
Understanding the feeling of his mind, Karkaṭa, the best of nāgas, / reported to Puṇḍarīka that lapse in his metrical cadence.
Hearing Karkoṭaka's words, Puṇḍarīka, the king of serpents, / his eyes red with anger, became exceedingly terrifying.
He cursed Lalita who was singing there, smitten with love: / 'Become a rākṣasa, O wicked-minded one, a carnivore and an eater of men!
Since you sang before me while under the influence of your wife!' / By his word, O lord of kings, he assumed the form of a rakṣas.
With a dreadful face, deformed eyes, terrifying merely at sight, / his arms extended a yojana wide, his mouth like a mountain cavern,
his two eyes like the moon and the sun, his neck like a mountain, / his nostrils two chasms, his lips stretching a yojana,
and his body, O king of kings, standing eight yojanas high. / Having become such a rākṣasa, he experienced the fruit of his deed.
Lalitā, however, seeing her husband thus deformed in shape, / pondered in her mind, tormented by great sorrow:
“What shall I do? Where shall I go? My husband is afflicted by a curse.” / Reflecting on this again and again, she found no peace in her mind.
Lalitā wandered with her husband in the dense forest; / that rākṣasa, changing his form at will, roamed in the impassable woods.
Pitiless, devoted to sin, deformed, a devourer of men, / afflicted by sin, he found no happiness by night or by day.
Lalitā, exceedingly sorrowful seeing her husband in such a state, / roamed with him, weeping, in the dense forest.
Seeing a charming hermitage and a sage of tranquil form, / Lalitā went swiftly, bowed down, and stood before him.
Seeing her distressed, that sage, full of compassion, said: / “Who are you? Why have you come here? Speak the truth before me.”
Lalitā said: / “There is a Gandharva named Vīradhanvan; know me to be the daughter of that great soul, / named Lalitā, who have come here on account of my husband.
By fault of sin my husband has become a rākṣasa, O great sage, / dreadful in form, of vile conduct; seeing him, I have no happiness.
Now instruct me, O brahmin; tell me what must be done, O lord.” / [The sage said:] “Perform that vow according to rule, O auspicious one, which is spoken by me.”
The sage said: / “It is now the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra, O woman with thighs like plantain stems; / there is the supreme Ekādaśī named Kāmadā, which destroys sin, O Lalitā.
Perform that vow, O auspicious one, according to rule as spoken by me; / whatever merit comes from this vow, let it be given to your husband.
When the merit is given, the fault of his curse will vanish in an instant.” / Having heard the sage’s words, Lalitā was filled with joy.
Having fasted on the Ekādaśī, O king, on the day of Dvādaśī, / right near the brahmin and before Vāsudeva,
Lalitā spoke these words for the deliverance of her husband: / “By me that vow of fasting on Kāmadā was indeed observed;
by the power of its merit, let his state of being a piśāca depart!” / Merely upon Lalitā’s words, even as he was there in that instant,
Lalita, freed from sin, came to possess a divine body; / his state of being a rākṣasa departed, and he attained his Gandharva nature again.
Adorned with gold and gems, he sported with Lalitā; / mounted upon an excellent aerial chariot, they were even more beautiful than their former forms.
The couple shone exceedingly through the power of Kāmadā. / Knowing this, O best of kings, this [vow] must be performed with exertion.
It has been related by me before you for the welfare of the worlds; / it destroys sins such as brahmin-killing and abolishes the state of being a piśāca.
There is nothing superior to this in the three worlds of the moving and unmoving; / from reciting or hearing it, O king, one obtains the fruit of a Vājapeya sacrifice.

6.48.m: Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, named "Kāmadā of the Bright Fortnight of Caitra," in the conversation between the husband of Umā and Nārada, in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the compilation of fifty-five thousand [verses].

6.49.m:
Yudhiṣṭhira said: / “In the dark fortnight of Vaiśākha, what is the name of the Ekādaśī? / Tell me its greatness, O Vāsudeva; homage to you!”

Yudhiṣṭhira said: / “In the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, what is the name of the Ekādaśī? / What is the fruit, what is the rule there? Tell me, O Janārdana!”

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Long ago, O king of kings, the wise Rāmacandra asked this very same question / to Vasiṣṭha, which you are now asking me.

Rāma said:
Lord, I wish to hear about the best vow among vows, / which destroys all sins and removes all sorrow.
I have experienced sorrows born of separation from Sītā; / therefore, filled with fear, I ask you, O great sage.

Vasiṣṭha said:
Well asked by you, O Rāma! Such is your resolute intellect; / merely by uttering your name a mortal becomes purified.
Nevertheless, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds, I shall describe / the pure among purifying things, the highest vow among vows.
In the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, O Rāma, there is an Ekādaśī; / it is celebrated by the name Mohinī, supreme, removing all sins.
People are released from the net of delusion and from heaps of sins / by the power of its vow; truly, truly do I say this.
For this reason, O Rāma, it ought to be observed by those like you; / it destroys sins and eradicates great sorrow.
Listen with focused mind, O Rāma, to the supreme tale that takes away sins, / by the mere hearing of which great sin is destroyed.
On the delightful bank of the Sarasvatī was the auspicious city of Bhadrāvatī; / there a king named Dyutimān indeed ruled the kingdom.
Born in the lunar lineage, steadfast, true to his word; / in that city lived a vaiśya, wealthy and prosperous in grain,
known as Dhanapāla, a promoter of meritorious deeds, / a builder of water booths, wells, monasteries, gardens, ponds, and rest-houses.
Devoted to Viṣṇu, peaceful, he had five sons: / Sumanas, Dyutimān, Medhāvin, Sukṛta,
and the fifth was Dhṛṣṭabuddhi, ever engaged in great sin, / constantly attached to the company of others' wives, an expert in gatherings of rogues.
Addicted to vices like gambling, craving intercourse with others' wives, / he had no thought for worshiping the gods, nor towards the ancestors, nor towards the twice-born.
Unjust in conduct, wicked-minded, squandering his father's wealth, / an eater of forbidden food, sinful, constantly engaged in drinking liquor;
with his arm around a harlot's neck, wandering vilely at crossroads, / he was cast out of the house by his father and abandoned by his relatives.
The ornaments of his own body were utterly brought to ruin by him; / he was abandoned by courtesans and reviled due to the loss of his wealth.
Then he became overcome with worry, stripped of clothes, tormented by hunger: / “What shall I do? Where shall I go? By what means can I survive?”
He took up thievery right in that city of his father; / he was seized by the king's men and released out of respect for his father.
Bound again, released again, bound again in haste; / the ill-behaved Dhṛṣṭabuddhi was bound fast with tight fetters,
struck with whip-lashes, and tormented repeatedly. / [The king said:] “O dull-witted one, you must not stay within the domain of my realm!”
Having spoken thus, he was released by the king from the firm bond; / out of fear of him, he departed and went to the dense forest.
Tormented by hunger and thirst, he ran hither and thither; / like a lion, he slew deer, boars, and spotted antelopes.
Constantly staying in the forest, intent on eating meat, / holding a bow in hand with a quiver attached to his back,
moving on foot, he killed the creatures that roam the forest and birds: / cakoras, peacocks, herons, partridges, and mice.
Blinded, the pitiless Dhṛṣṭabuddhi destroyed these and others; / sunk in the mire of sin due to sins committed in previous lives,
filled with sorrow and grief, tormented day and night, / he once reached the hermitage of Kauṇḍinya through the advent of merit.
In the month of Mādhava, afflicted by a burden of grief, / Dhṛṣṭabuddhi approached the ascetic who had bathed in the Gaṅgā.
By contact with drops of water from his garment, his sins departed and bad fortune was destroyed; / standing before Kauṇḍinya, he spoke with folded hands.

Dhṛṣṭabuddhi said:
O holy one, O best of the twice-born, have compassion on me; / tell me that through whose meritorious power liberation comes about.

Kauṇḍinya said:
Listen with an attentive mind to that by which your sin will be destroyed; / in the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha is the celebrated one named Mohinī.
Observe the vow of that Ekādaśī, urged by my word; / sins equal to Mount Meru meet destruction for embodied beings,
accumulated over many lifetimes, by those who fast on Mohinī. / Having heard this word of the sage, Dhṛṣṭabuddhi, with a gladdened heart,
performed the vow according to the rules, following Kauṇḍinya's instruction; / when the vow was performed, O best of kings, he became freed from sin.
Attaining a divine body, mounted upon Garuḍa, / he then went to the realm of Viṣṇu, free of all afflictions.
Such, O Rāmacandra, is the supreme vow of Mohinī; / there is nothing higher than this in the three worlds, movable and immovable.
Sacrifices, pilgrimages, and gifts do not equal a sixteenth part of it; / from reciting or hearing it, O king, one obtains the fruit of a thousand cows.

6.50.m:
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
What Ekādaśī is there in the dark fortnight of Jyeṣṭha? / I wish to hear its glorification; tell that, O Janārdana.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Well asked by you, O king, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds! / It indeed bestows much merit and destroys great sins.
It is named Aparā, O king of kings, boundless and granting sons; / whoever observes Aparā attains renown in the world.
Even one tainted by the murder of a brahmin, a slayer of his kinsman, a slayer of an embryo, / a slanderer of others, or one who takes pleasure in others' wives—
by observing Aparā, O king, he surely becomes free from sin. / One who gives false testimony, uses false measures, or cheats with the scale,
one who recites a fraudulent Veda, and likewise a fraudulent treatise, / a fraudulent astrologer, a fraudulent reckoner, or a fraudulent physician reciting the Veda,
joined with false testimony, should be recognized as an inhabitant of hell; / by observing Aparā, O king, they become liberated from sins.
A kṣatriya who abandons the duty of a kṣatriya and flees from battle / goes to a terrible hell, cast out from his own dharma;
by observing Aparā, he too, abandoning sin, goes to heaven. / Even an educated disciple who reviles his guru,
bound by great sins, goes to a frightful hell; / by observing Aparā, even that man attains a good state.
Hear the majesty of Aparā, O king, as I describe it: / the fruit men obtain at Prayāga when the sun is in Capricorn during Māgha,
the merit that is gained in Kāśī by bathing during an eclipse, / or the satisfaction given to the ancestors by offering the funerary ball at Gayā,
a man bathed in the Gautamī when the guru of the gods is in Leo, / or by plunging into the Kṛṣṇaveṇī when Jupiter is in Virgo, O king,
the fruit one obtains by beholding Kedāra during Kumbha, / or by journeying to the hermitage of Badarī and resorting to that sacred ford,
the fruit one obtains at Kurukṣetra during a solar eclipse / by giving gifts of elephants, horses, and gold, and performing a sacrifice with sacrificial fees—
Such fruit one obtains from observing the vow of Aparā. / Giving a cow half in birth, gold, and also land,
that fruit which a man obtains, he obtains through the vow of Aparā. / It is an axe to the tree of sin, a forest fire to the firewood of sin,
a sun to the darkness of sin, a lion to the deer of sin. / Like bubbles in water, like ants among living creatures,
they are born only to die, without the vow of Ekādaśī. / Having fasted on Aparā and worshipped Trivikrama,

freed from all sins, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu. / For the welfare of the worlds, this was told by me before you; / from reading and hearing it, O king, one obtains the fruit of a thousand cows.

6.51.m: Yudhiṣṭhira said: / All the glorification of Aparā has been heard, O Janārdana. / Tell me of that which falls in the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, O giver of honor.

The Blessed Kṛṣṇa said: / The righteous Vyāsa, son of Satyavatī, will speak of this— / he who knows the truth of the meaning of all treatises, who has crossed to the further shore of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: / The duties taught by Manu have been heard by me, and the duties taught by Vasiṣṭha have been heard by me. / O Dvaipāyana, you ought to speak properly of the Vaiṣṇava [duties].
The Blessed Vedavyāsa said: / The duties taught by Manu have been heard, and the Vedic duties have been heard by you; / but in the Kali age, they cannot be performed, O lord of men.
An easy means, of little expense, of little hardship, yielding great fruit, / and the very essence of all the Purāṇas, O great-minded one:
one should not eat on Ekādaśī in both fortnights. / Having become pure on Dvādaśī, having worshipped Keśava with flowers,
having shown hospitality, one should then eat food preceded by [feeding] brāhmaṇas. / One should not eat even in childbirth-impurity, nor in death-impurity, O lord of people.
Throughout life, this vow must be performed, O bull among men, / by those desiring to attain the heavenly path; of this there is no doubt.
Great sinners, evil-doers, the most wicked, devoid of dharma, / not eating on Ekādaśī, do not go into the presence of Yama.
Hearing those words of his, trembling like a leaf of the sacred fig tree, / the mighty-armed Bhīmasena bowed and spoke to the guru:
Bhīmasena said: / O grandfather of great intellect, hear my supreme word. / Yudhiṣṭhira, Kuntī, and also the daughter of Drupada,
Arjuna, Nakula, and also Sahadeva— / they never eat on Ekādaśī, being observers of good vows.
They always say to me indeed: 'Do not eat, O Vṛkodara!' / I tell them, O father: 'My hunger is unbearable.
I will give gifts according to rule, I will worship Keśava.' / Hearing Bhīmasena's words, Vyāsa spoke [this] word:
Vyāsa said: / If heaven is desired by you, and [to avoid] hell which is indeed terrible, / one must not eat on Ekādaśī in both fortnights.
Bhīmasena said: / O grandfather of great intellect, I speak before you: / I am able [only] with a single meal; how could there be fasting, O lord?
The fire named Vṛka is always in my belly; / only when I eat excessively does it subside.

I am not able to observe even a single fast, O great sage. / By whatever means heaven is attained, that I will do properly; / tell that one [vow] with certainty, by which I may attain the highest good.
Vyāsa said: / When Ekādaśī occurs while [the sun] is in Taurus or in Gemini / in the month of Jyeṣṭha, it should be fasted with effort, free from water.
Except for water for rinsing the mouth and sipping, a wise person / should not consume water at all here; otherwise, there would be a breach of the vow.
A man abstaining from water from sunrise to sunrise— / listen!—obtains the fruit of twelve Dvādaśīs.
Then, in the clear morning on Dvādaśī, he should take a bath, / and having given water and gold to the twice-born according to rule,
self-controlled, having accomplished his duty, he should eat together with brāhmaṇas. / And when this is done, hear the merit of that, O Bhīmasena:
Whatever Ekādaśīs occur indeed in the year, / he obtains the fruit of all of them; here there is no doubt in my mind.
“Thus Keśava, bearer of the conch, discus, and mace, spoke to me: / ‘Abandoning everything, a man should take refuge in me alone.’”
Without food on Ekādaśī, he is then freed from sin. / There is no purity of substances in the Kali age, nor traditional purificatory rites;
how could there even be Vedic [rites] when the corrupt Kali age has arrived? / What need to say much to you again and again, O son of Vāyu?
One should not eat on Ekādaśī in both fortnights. / On the Ekādaśī in the bright fortnight in the month of Jyeṣṭha, without water,
the meritorious fruit one obtains, hear that, O Vṛkodara: / whatever [Ekādaśīs] in a year are spoken of, bright and dark, O Vṛkodara,
all those Ekādaśīs indeed become fasted; of this there is no doubt. / Bestowing wealth and grain, holy, granting sons, health, and auspiciousness,
it is fasted, O tiger among men; thus I speak truth to you. / The messengers of Yama, huge-bodied, terrifying, dark in form,
bearing staff and noose, dread, do not approach that man. / Wearing yellow garments, gentle, with discuses in hand, swift as thought,
these lead Vaiṣṇavas to the city of Viṣṇu at the time of death. / Therefore, with all effort, [it is] to be fasted without water.
Giving a water-cow at that time, he is freed from all sins. / Therefore you, on this [day], O son of Kuntī, fasting, worshipping Hari,
act with all effort for the pacification of all sins. / 'Whether in sleep, may there be no offense by me, or through [food] entering my teeth;
I will eat food on the next day, O lord of gods, on the day of Hari.' / Uttering this mantra, one should then be intent on fasting,
for the destruction of all sins, endowed with faith and self-control. / Whatever sin as huge as Mount Meru or Mandara has been committed by a woman or man,
all that goes to ashes through the power of Ekādaśī. / Those who are unable to give a water-cow, O lord of men,
a water-pot with gold and cloth should be given. / Whoever undertakes the restriction of water on this [day] shares in merit.
The fruit of ten million [measures] of gold in every watch is heard as the fruit. / Bathing, giving, recitation of mantras, and offering oblations which a man performs on this [day]—
all that becomes imperishable; this was declared by Kṛṣṇa. / What need of any other dharma, without Nirjalā Ekādaśī?
Fasting properly according to rule, one attains the state of Viṣṇu. / Gold, food, or garment, whatever is given on this [day],
all that of his, O tiger of the Kurus, becomes imperishable. / He who eats food on the day of Ekādaśī eats sin;
in this world he is an outcaste, and dead, he meets an evil destiny. / And those who give gifts on Dvādaśī, having fasted,
in the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, will attain the supreme state. / The killer of a brāhmaṇa, a drinker of liquor, a thief, one who hates the guru, one who is always untruthful—
they are freed from all sins, having fasted on Nirjalā. / Hear the special duty, O son of Kuntī, on the day of Nirjalā Ekādaśī,
which is to be performed by men and women endowed with faith as a gift: / the One who reclines on the waters is to be worshipped, and a cow made of water is to be given.
Or an actual cow, O best of kings, or a cow made of ghee, / with well-nourished priestly fees and various kinds of sweet foods,
the twice-born should be zealously pleased, O best of upholders of dharma. / When the brahmins are pleased, Hari, the bestower of liberation, is indeed pleased through them.
Indeed, treason against oneself was committed by those by whom this [vow] was not observed; / they are sinful, ill-behaved, and robbed—there is no doubt of this.
A hundred future generations and likewise a hundred past generations / are brought along with themselves to the abode of Vāsudeva
by those who are peaceful, self-controlled, devoted to charity, and worshipping Hari, / keeping a vigil through the night, by whom this [vow] is observed.
Food, clothing, cows, water, a bed, an auspicious seat, / a water pot, and an umbrella should be given on the day without water.
Whoever gives a pair of shoes to an eminent, worthy twice-born / is honored in the heavenly realm upon a golden chariot.
Whoever hears this with devotion and whoever proclaims it— / both of them attain heaven; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
Whatever fruit a mortal obtains by performing an ancestral rite at Saṃnihitā / when the sun is seized by Rāhu, he obtains that even from hearing this.
And the vow should be undertaken after first cleansing one’s teeth: / 'On the eleventh day, fasting, I shall certainly abstain from water,
for the sake of pleasing Keśava, with no other [water] except for sipping.' / On the twelfth day, Trivikrama, the lord of the gods, should be worshipped
with perfumes, incense, flowers, and lovely garments; / having worshipped according to the rules, one should utter this mantra:
'O god of gods, O Hṛṣīkeśa, O savior from the ocean of worldly existence, / lead me to the supreme goal by this gift of a water-jar.'
Indeed, in the month of Jyeṣṭha, O Bhīma, the bright eleventh day is auspicious; / having fasted without water on it, [and] water-jars with sugar
having given to the foremost brahmins, one rejoices in the presence of Viṣṇu. / Then water-jars should be given to brahmins with devotion;
having fed the brahmins, one should then eat oneself, fully devoted. / Whoever thus fulfills the sin-destroying twelfth day

is freed from all sins and goes to the sorrowless abode. / From that time onward, this auspicious eleventh day was observed by Bhīma; / it indeed became known in the world by the name Pāṇḍava-dvādaśī.

Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, named the Nirjalā Ekādaśī of the bright half of Jyeṣṭha, in the dialogue between the Lord of Umā and Nārada, in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand [verses].

6.52.m: Yudhiṣṭhira said: / In the dark fortnight of Āṣāḍha, which eleventh day indeed occurs? / Please tell me by your grace, O Vāsudeva, in my presence.
The blessed Kṛṣṇa said: / O king, I shall tell you the foremost of vows, / which destroys all sins and bestows all liberation.
In the dark fortnight of Āṣāḍha is the eleventh day named Yoginī, / O best of kings, which destroys great sins,
serving as an eternal boat for those drowned in the ocean of worldly existence, / the essential substance in the three worlds for those who perform the Yoginī vow.
I shall tell you an auspicious puranic tale: / In Alakā was the king of kings [Kubera], devoted to the worship of Śiva.
He had a flower-gathering page named Hemamālin. / His wife was beautiful and named Viśālākṣī.
His mind was attached to her, falling under the sway of love's snare. / Having brought a collection of lotuses from Lake Mānasa, he stayed in his own house.
Clinging to the sweet nectar of love for his wife, he did not go to Kubera’s dwelling. / Kubera was performing the worship of Śiva in the temple of the god.
At noon, O king, while [Kubera was] waiting for the arrival of the flowers, / Hemamālin was sporting with his beloved in his own house.
Then the king of the yakṣas, angered by the passing of the appointed time, said: / 'Why does the wicked Hemamālin not come, O yakṣas? / Ascertain this!' he said again and again.
The yakṣas said: / 'Desiring his woman, he sports in his home as he pleases, O king.' / Hearing their words, Kubera was filled with rage.
He quickly summoned the servant Hemamālin. / Realizing the delay of time, his eyes agitated with fear,
he came without even bathing and stood before Kubera. / Seeing him, the giver of wealth [Kubera] was enraged, his eyes reddened with fury.
Overcome with anger, his lip trembling with rage, he replied. / Dhanada said: / 'Ah, sinful, wicked, ill-behaved one, you have shown contempt for the god!
Stricken with the eighteen kinds of leprosy, separated from that beloved woman, / fallen from this place, go now to a wretched state, vile one!'
When those words were spoken, he fell down from that spot, / overcome by immense misery, his body afflicted with leprosy.
He had no comfort by day and found no sleep at night; / his body was tormented in the shade and exceedingly tormented in the heat of summer.
By the power of his worship of Śiva, his memory was not lost; / though overwhelmed by his sin, he remembered his past deeds.
Wandering about, he then went to Himādri, the best of mountains; / there he saw the eminent sage Mārkaṇḍeya, a treasure of asceticism,
whose lifespan, O king, was equal to the age of Brahmā. / The doer of evil deeds saluted his feet from afar.
Seeing him trembling thus, Mārkaṇḍeya, the best of sages, / summoned him for the sake of helping others, and spoke this:
'Why are you stricken with leprosy? Why are you utterly blameworthy?' / Thus addressed, he replied to the great sage Mārkaṇḍeya.
Hemamālin said: / 'I am an attendant of the king of kings, named Hemamālin. / Having fetched a collection of lotuses daily from Lake Mānasa, O sage,
I offer them to Kubera at the time of Śiva’s worship. / On one day, the time went unnoticed by me,
as I was attached to the pleasure of my wife, my mind agitated by grief. / Then, O sage, I was cursed by the angered king of kings.
I became stricken with leprosy and separated from that beloved woman. / Now, through some meritorious deed, I have come into your presence.
By nature, the mind of the virtuous is capable of helping others. / Knowing this, O best of sages, instruct me, who have committed an offense.'
Mārkaṇḍeya said: / 'Since you have spoken truth here and have not uttered untruth, / therefore I shall tell you the instruction on a vow that brings auspiciousness.
Observe the Yoginī vow in the dark fortnight of Āṣāḍha; / by the religious merit of this vow, your leprosy will surely disappear.'
Hearing the words of the sage, he fell like a staff upon the ground; / raised up by the sage, he became exceedingly joyful.
When the vow was performed by him as instructed by Mārkaṇḍeya, / his eighteen leprosies vanished completely.
By the word of the sage, when the vow was properly observed, he became happy. / In this manner, O best of kings, the Yoginī vow has been narrated.
The man who performs the Yoginī vow / obtains a fruit equal to that of one who feeds eighty-eight thousand twice-born.
It pacifies great sins and bestows the fruit of great religious merit; / from reading it and hearing it, a mortal is freed from all sins.

Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, named the Glorification of the Yoginī Ekādaśī of the dark half of Āṣāḍha, in the dialogue between the Lord of Umā and Nārada, in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand [verses].

6.53.m:
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Which ekādaśī occurs in the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha? / What is its name, and what is its rite? Tell this in detail.

Lord Kṛṣṇa said:
I will tell [you] of the supremely meritorious [ekādaśī], bestower of heaven and liberation, / named Śayanī, supreme, remover of all sins,
merely by hearing of which one obtains the fruit of a Vājapeya sacrifice. / Truly, truly have I declared: there is nothing higher than this for human beings.
It was created by the Creator for the destruction of sinners' sins, most exalted; / beyond this, O king of kings, there is none other that grants liberation.
For this reason, O king, let it be heard; the highest destination / shall be attained by men who listen even to the hearing of this tale.
They are ever Vaiṣṇavas, O king, wholly devoted to my bhakti. / In Āṣāḍha, indeed, the Supreme Lord Vāmana is worshipped.
By whoever Vāmana, the lotus-eyed, is worshipped with lotuses / in the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha on the day of Kāmikā,
by him the entire universe and the three eternal gods are worshipped, / and by him the ekādaśī, the highest day of Hari, has been observed.

Yudhiṣṭhira said:
I have a great doubt in this matter; listen, O Puruṣottama: / How did you fall asleep, O Lord of gods, and how did you take refuge with Bali?
And how did you lie down upon the earth? What do other people do? / Tell me this, O greatly wise one; I have a great doubt.

Lord Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O tiger among kings, to the supreme tale that removes sin, / merely by hearing of which the destruction of all sins occurs.
Formerly in the Tretā age, O king, there was a daitya named Bali, / who constantly worshipped me, devoted to me, intent upon me.
With sacrifices according to rule, the daitya worshipped me, the eternal one, / and with supreme devotion, O king, he was an agent of sacrifices and performer of vows.
Having deliberated at length with Indra and with hymns of praise, / and together with the preceptor and the gods, I was worshipped in many ways.
Then, in the form of Vāmana, in my fifth incarnation, / assuming a most formidable form, embodying the entire universe,
the daityas were overcome through a trick of speech, while he stood firm relying on truth. / Śukra warned him, saying, 'This is Nārāyaṇa.'
Land measuring three and a half strides was begged by me, O king; / and as soon as the water of solemn resolve was placed in [my] hand by him,
hear, O king, the kind of form I assumed then: / placing the feet on the earth-world, and the knees on the atmospheric world;
placing the waist on the heavenly world, and the belly likewise on Maharloka; / the heart on Janaloka, and the neck on Tapoloka;
establishing the face on Satyaloka, and the head above it. / The moon, the sun, the planets, and likewise the lunar mansions,
the gods with Indra, the nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and kinnaras / praised [me] with various hymns born from the Vedas.
Taking Bali by the hand, the earth was encompassed in three strides, / and then half a stride was placed by me upon his back.
The dānava, my worshipper, went to the underworld, O king. / The dānava was cast below; what did they do after that?
Bent with humility, he [pleased] Janārdana, who became exceedingly gracious. / In the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha is the Kāmikā day of Hari.
One form of mine stands relying on Bali; / a second [reclines] upon the back of Śeṣa in the midst of the ocean of milk.
He sleeps in this way, O great king, until the coming Kārtikī. / Until then, one should become truly righteous, foremost among all performers of dharma.
And a mortal who performs this vow goes to the supreme state. / For this reason, O king, it should be observed with diligent effort.
There is nothing higher than this, purifying and destroying sins, / on which the Lord of the gods, bearer of the conch, discus, and mace, sleeps.
And on that day one should worship the god bearing the conch, discus, and mace, / keeping an all-night vigil, and doing so especially with devotion.
Even the four-faced [Brahmā] is unable to calculate its merit. / The person who thus observes the supreme vow of the eleventh day, O king,
which removes all sins and bestows enjoyment and liberation, / is ever dear to me in this world, even if he be a dog-cooker.
Those who spend the four months here by offering lamps, / eating from leaves of the palāśa tree, and observing vows, are dear to me.
During the four months, while Hari is asleep, a person should sleep on the bare ground. / In Śrāvaṇa one should avoid greens, and likewise curd in Bhādrapada.
Milk is to be abandoned in Āśvayuja, and pulses must be abandoned in Kārtika; / or, remaining steadfast in celibacy, he goes to the supreme state.
Only by the vow of the eleventh day is a man freed from sins. / It must always be performed, O king, and never forgotten.
Whatever dark eleventh day falls between the sleeping one and the waking one, / that alone should be fasted on by a householder, no other dark [eleventh day] ever.
And whatever man listens, O king, to this supreme tale that takes away sins, / he obtains the fruit of the horse sacrifice.

Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, named the Devaśayanī Ekādaśī, in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara, in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand [verses].
